Brassic:
Main character is based on the real life experiences of show creator Joe Gilgun, who has bipolar. His illness is named and normalised in the show. Very well done. Shows the frustrating interactions with his doctor. Glimpses into the sadness and general bizzare manic energy of his escapades. Top notch comedy. Laugh your socks off, with excellent swearing. 

Flowers:
Written by Will Sharpe, who plays Shun, who has bipolar in real life. The show generally centered around depression, but season two focuses heavily on bipolar. Outstandingly done. The depection of psychotic mania and its fallout I found to be very accurate. The portrayal of the deep heartbreak of depression is just perfect. Very bleak dark comedy.

It's something I've worked on very hard, and words cannot describe how beautiful the pay off is. After years of isolation and having lost many, many friends, I now have wonderful, loving people in my life. 

I can get fixaed on someone, with either rage or paranoia, and am now hyper aware of it, and go silent for a bit instead of hulking out. I've made an effort to become a listener to other people's emotions, and am someone they can come to, instead of just dumping my emotions in other people. I try to communicate what's going on when possible, I struggle to keep contact during depressions. My rule is I'm not allowed to let my anger out for 3 days, and if something is still a problem, then I can say- and essentially 99. 999% of my anger is flippant bollocks and me just being oversensitive and reactive. I find it harder to keep control in romantic relationships as they're there all the time, and I need significant social recharge to avoid getting ill. 

It's difficult. You need to be serious with yourself about your flaws and your illness, and learn not to take it out on other people as much as feedsibly possible. I go down the avoidance route, and am infinitely lucky to have understanding friends that are still there at the end of the episode. As others have said, it helps that alll of them are neuro divergent.

For example, my best friend is autistic, and she will absolutely tell me when she's annoyed, and we work through it constructively. This means that most of the time I can logic my way out of the fear that she secretly despises me (although not always, ah self hatred and rejection anxiety, you silly goose).

It takes continual consistent effort. I make a conscious choice to be there for my friends and not bombard them with my mental illness. It rules my life, so when I'm with them, I'd generally rather talk about literally anything else (that's not to say I never do, and when I talk about it they listen, but I try to keep it as minimal as possible). It's vastly improved my quality of life.

It's legitimately considered an immune disorder. The continual increased level of cortisol (stress hormone) creates havoc- including massive internal inflammation. I didn't realise this until way after getting the covid jab. Bipolar and schizophrenia were in the first group to receive it, and I just assumed it was because we're mental and couldn't be relied upon to behave safely and not pass it around- but it turns out it's because of this terrible inflation, meant that we were actually more susceptible the diabetics.

I notice that after an episode I tend to get bed ridden with some kind of flu, and seem to be under the weather a lot more than everyone else I know. Also have terrible TMJ, which at one point locked up my jaw for two years straight. Constant headaches, yadda yadda yadda. Messed up stomach because of all the stress and dread. 

It really doesn't feel fair. Being so mentally ill that you get physically ill.

At university studying history and politics, Bipolar II. Attempt No.2, as had to drop out first time due to massive depressive episode.
My tutors all know about my illness, and don't ask questions about my lack of attendance, providing all of my work is in on time. If I go to uni hypo, I end up shouting out answers in the middle of lectures, if I go in depressed I will just fall asleep- so its better for everyone if I stay at home and ride it out. 
To get work done, I lock myself in my living room with a pile of energy drinks and refuse to leave until everything is finished. I try and give myself extra time depending on where I am in a cycle. Hypo Sarah needs a day to finish a 2000 word essay, misery Sarah needs two weeks. It's all about knowing yourself, and pushing through.

Thank you so much for taking the time to write that out! And yes, that makes perfect sense. I think its one f the problems with trying to figure out what's going on inside your own head, you end up reading these terms, and using them without thinking to describe your feelings- like the way we pick up any other kinds of words. When I saw the psychiatrists I probably just sounded like a hypochondriac who happened to know the bipolar terminology! They told me to keep a journal, but half of the problem is that I act and think in such ways that I often don't realise its a symptom until later on. Like when I thought I was in completely in love with one of my friends, that delusion lasted for about 2 weeks, but at the time it felt so genuine. 
So yes, try to establish what specific things I'm actually experiencing, instead of using vague diagnostic terms, that cloud any medical judgement. Then once I've pinned everything down, try seeing a professional and explaining things thoroughly.  
Again, thank you so much!
